newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria's pro-government party confident after poll.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's pro-government party confident after poll.

text.p: Algeria's pro-government party said on Friday it was doing well as results of the first general election in five years of violence began to trickle in.
But the National Democratic Rally (RND) did not give any figures and officials were not releasing any early results.

The election was the first since Moslem fundamentalists dominated a December 1991 poll. The military-backed authorities cancelled that election in January 1992 and shortly afterwards the country plunged into violence in which an estimated 60,000 people died.
Algiers state radio said voter turnout in Thursday's election stood at 66.30 percent, or 10.6 million people, but the figure did not include the turnout of Algerians voting outside the country.
A total of 16.8 million Algerians are eligible to vote.
The radio said Interior Minister Mustapha Benmansour would declare the final results "after" 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Friday.
"We are in a very respectable position," RND spokesman Hamraoui Habib Chawki told Reuters. "The results that we have from the various provinces put the party constantly in the top three positions."
But Chawki hinted that the party would not be able to gain an absolute majority in the 380-seat National Assembly, the lower house.
"From now on there will not be any single dominant force. This will help the development of democracy and diversify the lower house," he said.
A new proportional representation law makes it very difficult for a single party to gain an absolute majority.
Security was tight at polling stations which opened at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Thursday as voters cast ballots to choose from more than 7,000 candidates representing 39 political parties.
A bomb wrecked a car carrying observers supervising the poll, seriously wounding two local monitors, sources at a party contesting the elections said.
The blast followed a wave of bombings in the capital Algiers by suspected Moslem rebels that killed 22 people in the run up to the election.
The U.S. State Department praised voters for turning out in force, saying they had shown "courage because they have been subjected to the most vicious case of terrorism over many, many years".
"I voted for peace," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, said after he and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El- Warda school in the capital's Telemly neighbourhood.
The government of President Liamine Zeroual says the poll is a key step towards ending the civil strife.

Sceptics in the Algerian capital doubt the level of violence would soon drop because the new assembly will be deprived of any real power and will not be able to start a dialogue with radical Islamists.

The RND's main competitors include the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of moderate Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
Several party leaders complained of irregularities at the election but Interior Minister Benmansour dismissed the complaints as "political competition".
"Algeria does not allow itself to permit -- even by local authorities -- such irregularities," he said.
Shortly before polls closed, Arab League monitors said the elections were proceeding in a fair and free atmosphere.
The 61 Arab observers are among some 200 monitors from the United States, Europe, Africa and the Middle East.
